Trump says planned 250-foot arch will be ‘military complex’ for drones, snipers
President Donald Trump on Sunday said his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch will now be a “top grade” military complex that will house drones, snipers and ammunition, in a social media post that raised new questions about the controversial project.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that he has agreed to convert the arch “at the strong request” of the U.S. military, and “for National Security purposes.”
The “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” near Arlington National Cemetery will “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump wrote. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.”
Trump and his deputies had previously maintained that the arch would be a new tourist attraction, and the administration has released detailed plans of its internal design and outside observation deck. The administration had not previously broached the idea of converting the arch to a military complex, even as the project has undergone months of federally required reviews.
The Trump administration plans to begin construction on the arch as soon as November, amid resistance from military veterans, advocacy groups and historic preservationists who say the towering structure will overshadow the nearby cemetery and is too large for the site. A federal judge is weighing whether to halt the project.
On Sunday, some critics asked whether the arch would now undergo further required reviews to accommodate Trump’s new vision.
“Presumably, this would result in security hardening, inclusive of fencing, guard posts, and other additional features above and beyond what has been approved,” Charles Birnbaum, the CEO of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, wrote in an email to the Commission of Fine Arts, which approved the arch in May. The email was shared with The Washington Post.
Critics also questioned the practicality of building a military complex at the center of a widely used traffic circle not far from Reagan National Airport.
The White House did not respond to questions about the president’s post, including the need for a military complex at the arch site. The Interior Department, which oversees the federal parkland where the arch would be built, did not reply to requests for comment, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond the president’s post.
Trump’s new claims about the arch resemble his arguments for the need to build a ballroom at the White House. Trump initially said the ballroom was needed to entertain guests but more recently has said it was a “desperately needed National Security structure.” That argument also has become central to the administration’s legal claims that the ballroom must be built.
Trump has spent nearly a year touting his plans to build an arch at Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout tucked inside Washington’s boundaries, near the entrance to the military cemetery and managed by the National Park Service.
The president and his deputies have said the arch should be built to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. The administration contends it does not need congressional approval for the arch because lawmakers a century ago authorized a somewhat similar project near the site.
“This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X this month.
The Trump administration has acknowledged that its arch project will alter pedestrians’ views of the Lincoln Memorial and other historic sites, affect the experience of visiting Arlington National Cemetery and cause other disruptions.
A D.C. official last week advised the administration to abandon its plans and instead pursue a less obtrusive alternative.
Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia), who represents the district that encompasses the cemetery and National Airport, has also urged Trump to stop the project and seek authorization from Congress before building a structure.
“Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” Beyer wrote Sunday, suggesting on X that it was a pretext to strengthen Trump’s legal arguments for the arch.
Outside lawyers also questioned Trump’s national security claims.
“The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” said Nicolas Sansone, a lawyer at Public Citizen Litigation Group, a watchdog organization that is representing several veterans who say the large arch would alter their experience when visiting the nearby military cemetery.
U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, the Obama administration appointee who is reviewing the veterans’ case, has warned the Trump administration not to abruptly move forward with construction on the arch - as Trump did when demolishing the White House’s East Wing to build his ballroom without seeking approval from federal review panels or from Congress.
Trump officials have said they will obtain “all necessary approvals” before beginning construction on the arch.
The president’s claim Sunday about the arch being converted to a military complex follows his administration’s evolving legal strategy to defend the ballroom on similar grounds.
Administration officials have increasingly contended that the ballroom must be built by citing the planned military complex being constructed underneath it and the need to protect the president.
Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, said the administration’s national security claims in the ballroom case had merit.
“The equities in this case turn on complex architectural and security determinations best made by the Secret Service and the military - not judges,” Rao wrote in August.
Other federal judges have said that Trump could not claim broad national security reasons as a basis to pursue a construction project that had not been authorized by Congress.
“While I take seriously the Government’s concerns regarding the safety and security of the White House grounds and the President himself, the existence of a ‘large hole’ beside the White House is, of course, a problem of the President’s own making,” U.S. District Judge Richard Leon - who first blocked work on the ballroom - wrote earlier this year.
The Supreme Court on Aug. 31 ruled 5-4 that construction on the ballroom could continue for now but declined to rule on the merits of the administration’s arguments in that case.

President Donald Trump said that he plans to make his proposed 250-foot arch in Washington, DC, a “top grade military complex” that holds large stores of weaponry, citing national security reasons and a “strong request” from the US military.
Trump added in his Sunday post on Truth Social that the planned “Triumphal Arch” near the National Mall would “have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas.”
The president first proposed building the arch last October to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary. The much-criticized project, as currently planned, would tower over most other DC landmarks—the tallest being the Washington Monument, at approximately 555 feet—and block the view of Arlington National Cemetery from the Lincoln Memorial.
Three Vietnam War veterans sued the administration to prevent construction of the arch based on the view issue, and also because Trump has not secured the required approval from Congress. Earlier this month, a federal judge ordered the administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before doing any work on the project, but has yet to rule on the merits of the case.
Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) called Trump’s new arch plan, “obviously idiotic” as he “clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security.”
Trump’s latest post represents a significant departure from his former plan for the arch, which included a winged, gilded statue of Lady Liberty and an inscription reading, “One Nation Under God.” The drones and snipers could indeed be a matter of Trump trying to justify the arch as a national security requirement—he applied a similar argument to his unpermitted and unpopular White House ballroom, announcing in March that “the military is building a big complex under the ballroom.”
As my colleague Sophie Hurwitz has pointed out, Trump has a long history of using the idea of “national security” to do whatever he wants: threatening to annex Greenland, targeting ICE protesters as terrorists, expanding construction of hyperscale data centers, and removing trans people from public life. “If national security is everything, then national security is nothing at all,” Hurwitz noted. Well, except, in this case, an excuse for Trump to abuse his power when no one is willing to stop him.

Trump wants to use Washington arch as military complex for drones and snipers
Donald Trump says the planned 76-metre arch near Washington doubles as a military complex with drones and snipers, though he gives no specific threat.
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday (Sep 20) the triumphal arch he plans to build near Washington would double as a "military complex" housing drones and snipers, making it the second major construction project he has sought to justify on national security grounds.
The move, which Trump said came at the military's request, echoed the national security rationale he has used to defend the roughly US$400 million ballroom complex being built on the site of the White House's former East Wing. He did not identify any specific threats.
The arch and ballroom are part of Trump's broader effort to remake the nation's capital, including the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the redevelopment of a golf course in East Potomac Park, and a push to add his name to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The initiatives have drawn criticism from preservationists and others who argue they would alter some of Washington's most prominent historic landmarks.
In a social media post, Trump said that at the "strong request" of the military he had agreed to turn the planned 76-meter arch "into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage."
A US military official told Reuters that the Defense Department had nothing to add beyond Trump's social media post. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump did not elaborate on why such capabilities would be needed at the arch, modeled on Paris' Arc de Triomphe and sited near Arlington National Cemetery, just across the Potomac River from Washington. He has similarly recast the ballroom as a national security project, with plans for a drone facility, bomb shelters and other military installations intended to protect Washington.
EXPERT QUESTIONS MILITARY RATIONALE
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel, said that while there was a stronger case for enhancing security at the White House, including expanding underground bunker facilities, the rationale for militarizing the arch was harder to discern.
Cancian said the move appeared aimed at countering opposition to the monument, which is planned for a traffic circle just 1 mile (1.6 km) from Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, an active Army installation, and 2 miles from the Pentagon.
"It looks like it's tacked on in order to strengthen the rationale for construction," Cancian, a senior adviser with the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, told Reuters. "There is this military facility long established with a variety of military capabilities one mile away. So why you need this one isn't clear."
Cancian also said that storing ammunition at the arch would create logistical challenges and questioned the value of positioning snipers there.
LEGAL CHALLENGES MOUNT
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan earlier this month ordered the Trump administration to give 48 hours' notice before engaging in any activity on the site of the arch, which Trump proposed to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. Her ruling came a day after the Interior Department announced plans to move forward with work on the arch despite legal challenges and the lack of final approval from a government planning authority.
Aviation experts have raised safety concerns given its proximity to Reagan Washington National Airport while veterans have sued to block the arch, arguing it would destroy the carefully designed historic sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
The Federal Aviation Administration said last week that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as the structure is topped with an "eternal flame."
US Representative Don Beyer, a Democrat whose Virginia district includes Arlington National Cemetery, posted on Sunday that operating drones so close to the airport would be dangerous and impractical, and suggested the move was aimed at bolstering the administration's legal position.
"Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security," Beyer, who has introduced legislation to block the arch's construction, wrote in a social media post.

President Trump announced on Sunday morning that his planned triumphal arch in Washington DC will now serve as a “top-grade military complex,” as reported by The Guardian. This shift in the project scope arrives following what the President described as the “strong request” of the US military.
The structure was originally framed as a monument to national greatness. The new design for the 250ft granite arch will feature specialized capabilities, including drone storage and ammunition facilities.
The President noted that the structure will be able to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage. He also confirmed that the roof and plaza will be equipped with customised sniper facilities. The President is leaning into the extreme utility of this build, as he claimed, “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world.”
This project is slated to begin construction this month
The President has tied the arch to the upcoming 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. He maintains that it will be “by far the greatest triumphal arch” in any of the world’s top cities and capitals. The aesthetic design remains consistent with his previous vision, featuring granite cladding and three golden statues positioned on top.
The location of this arch has been a major point of contention for some time. It is intended to sit in a circle near the Memorial Bridge, a spot that critics argue will ruin the sight lines of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
The National Park Service recently issued a warning regarding the project, stating that it could have adverse effects to historic properties. They have requested further planning before any construction moves forward. Additionally, the proximity of the site to the Ronald Reagan Washington International Airport has raised concerns among Democratic Congress members.
This arch is just one piece of a broader series of construction efforts that the President has pushed to change the visual landscape of the capital. These initiatives include the renovation of the Kennedy Center, the refurbishment of the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial, and the creation of a White House ballroom.
The White House ballroom has also been referred to by the President as a military complex. That specific project faced significant legal challenges before the US Supreme Court finally cleared the path for work to proceed last month.
Many of these projects have struggled with structural issues, legal hurdles, and intense criticism regarding their overall aesthetic appeal. Some observers see these endeavors as attempts by the President to cement his own legacy. The situation at the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has been particularly tense. After courts blocked his attempt to add his name to the title of the venue, the President suggested he might move to demolish the building entirely.

Trump Says Planned 250-Foot Washington Arch Will Double as Drone and Sniper Military Complex
The proposed monument near the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery faces objections over aviation safety, presidential authority and damage to a historic landscape
President Donald Trump says a planned 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington DC will double as a military facility, with space to store and deploy drones and positions for snipers, after what he called the 'strong request' of the US military. Announcing the changes on Truth Social, he said the additions were driven by national security considerations.
The arch is planned for Memorial Circle in Lady Bird Johnson Park, along the route connecting the Lincoln Memorial with Arlington National Cemetery. The Pentagon said it had no further details beyond Trump's post, while the White House declined to comment.
Lawmakers warn that operating military drones directly along Reagan National Airport's flight path poses air safety risks. Vietnam veterans also argue the president lacks authority to construct the monument, claiming it defaces the historic landscape surrounding Arlington National Cemetery.
Democrat Calls Drone Site 'Dangerous' Near Airport
The proposal has drawn criticism from US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat. Beyer objected to the planned drone site because of its location near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. He said the proposed launch site would be dangerous and unworkable because it would sit in the airport's flight approach path.
The arch is the second major Washington construction project Trump has described in military terms. He previously referred to a planned $400 million expansion of the White House ballroom as an underground 'military complex'. The scale of the proposed arch would make it a major new feature of the capital's skyline.
Towering Arch Would Dominate Capital Skyline
A preliminary National Park Service report puts the total height at about 250 feet. The main structure would rise roughly 166 feet, with statuary and other elements making up the remaining height.
The arch would have a 91‑foot by 166‑foot footprint and a 55‑foot‑wide central opening. Inside, there would be 70,072 gross square feet spread across five occupiable levels.
An observation deck at 161 feet 6 inches would include about 9,812 square feet of exterior space. That would make the arch more than twice the height of the 99‑foot Lincoln Memorial and roughly half the height of the Washington Monument.
Plans call for granite from Vermont, North Carolina or California, with black granite paving and bronze, antique bronze and gold statuary. Among the proposed features are a winged crown figure, golden eagles and golden lions.
Lawsuit Argues President Lacks Authority to Build
The project is also facing a legal challenge from three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian.
Their lawsuit argues that the president cannot build a major monument in the capital without congressional authorisation. It also claims the arch would damage the grounds of Arlington National Cemetery and interfere with the historic vista between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.
The lawsuit says the sightline was deliberately designed after the Civil War to symbolise the country coming back together. US District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan has ordered the administration to give 48 hours' notice before construction or excavation begins.
Park Service Flags Historic and Environmental Concerns
The National Park Service has raised its own concerns about the design. It warned that the project could have an adverse impact on historic properties, including the Memorial Avenue Corridor Cultural Landscape and Arlington Memorial Bridge.
The project would add about 62,875 square feet of impervious surface. To manage the resulting stormwater, around 6,300 cubic feet would need to be retained on site through bioretention rain gardens. There are also archaeological concerns.
An assessment found moderate‑to‑high sensitivity for intact precolonial and historic remains beneath 10 to 14 feet of fill. New water, sewer, electric and gas lines would also have to be extended across nearby roads and bridges.
Despite the concerns about the airport, the Federal Aviation Administration found that the arch would not create a hazard for aircraft.
The FAA also concluded that it would have no significant effect on flight procedures or navigational aids. It did, however, require obstruction lighting at the top of the structure. Earlier site and visual designs had received approval from the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission.
Visitors Would Face Airport-Style Security Screening
The exterior plaza would remain open to the public under the NPS plans, while access to the interior would use timed entry, similar to the system at the Washington Monument. Visitors would face security screening, including walk‑through magnetometers, X‑ray equipment and explosive trace detection.
The planned system is expected to process about 20 people every 15 minutes, making security the main potential bottleneck for visitors. Vehicles would be kept out of the plaza except for authorised maintenance, law enforcement and emergency access. Bollards, a barricade seat wall and continuous video surveillance are also planned around the site.
